title: Value-Rectified Distillation for Flow-based Offline Reinforcement Learning

paper.title: Value-Rectified Distillation for Flow-based Offline Reinforcement Learning
paper.abstract: Abstract We aim to address the problem of Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Mode Averaging , a critical problem that emerges when distilling Flow Matching (FM) based behavior policies in offline Reinforcement Learning (RL): When learning over multi-modal datasets, standard distillation inadvertently forces the policy to interpolate across different behavioral modes, causing the generated actions to collapse into invalid, OOD regions. To resolve this, we propose Value-Rectified Distillation (VRD) , a novel framework that reformulates offline policy distillation as a value-guided generative trajectory alignment problem. By employing a dynamic coupling mechanism, VRD actively rectifies flow dynamics to explicitly decouple distinct behavioral modes, cleanly isolating high-value actions. Specifically, we instantiate VRD through two complementary algorithms: VRD-Q , which utilizes value-quantile behavior distillation to statistically filter out low-value behaviors, and VRD-R , which reorganizes the latent space to geometrically isolate high-value generative trajectories from the FM-based behavior policy. Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that VRD improves existing generative baselines across diverse continuous control and planning tasks on the D4RL, OGBench, and Minari benchmarks, especially over those multi-modal, non-expert datasets.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) aims to derive a high-capacity policy from a fixed, pre-collected dataset without further environment interaction [ 17 , 15 ] , which is particularly vital for the applications where online exploration is costly or hazardous. Recently, generative models, particularly Flow Matching (FM) [ 18 ] , have emerged as a powerful alternative to traditional Diffusion-based methods [ 9 , 2 , 5 ] , where FM-based policies, such as Flow Q-Learning (FQL) [ 21 ] , offer significant advantages in modeling complex, multi-modal behavior distributions while circumventing the training instabilities typically associated with backpropagating through ODE solvers. Figure 1: Problem of Latent Fusion (left) and the OOD Mode Averaging problem caused by FQL-style behavior distillation (right). Despite their empirical promise, we identify a fundamental pathology in how current flow-based RL frameworks distill high-value actions from multi-modal behavior policies. Specifically, when learning from multi-modal data, our analysis reveals that Flow Matching networks inherently suffer from Latent Fusion : the topological entanglement between the generative trajectories of optimal and sub-optimal behavioral modes, caused by the vector field’s training dynamics, as is shown in Figure 1 (left). In previous works, like FQL [ 21 ] , it first pre-trains a behavior flow policy to capture the full multi-modal behavior distribution [ 4 ] from the dataset, and subsequently applies Q-value guidance to distill the optimal policy. However, because such distillation operates on a continuous vector field where trajectories are already topologically entangled by the MLE pre-training, the Q-guided objective, as is shown in Figure 1 (right), inadvertently forces the sampled actions to linearly interpolate across distinct modes during inference, which triggers the OOD Mode Averaging disaster, where it is risky for the generated actions to collapse into low-density regions of the state-action manifold, ultimately causing performance degradation. Although recent approaches like Guided Flow Policy (GFP) [ 24 ] incorporate reward information to amplify optimal behavior modes in FM-based behavior policy, their FQL-style distillation mechanism still suffers from OOD Mode Averaging . To address this issue, our core insight is that during the distillation phase, policy refinement must go beyond simply cloning from FM-based behavior policy; rather, it inherently requires rectifying the flow dynamics to explicitly decouple distinct behavioral modes along the data manifold. Therefore, we introduce Value-Rectified Distillation (VRD) , a novel framework that reformulates offline policy distillation as a value-guided trajectory alignment problem, of which the core lies in a dynamic coupling mechanism that precisely modulates the flow dynamics to explicitly decouple and exclude sub-optimal behavioral modes, ensuring that the generated actions are confined to the optimal action manifold during inference. To instantiate this unified framework, we derive two distinct algorithms from complementary mathematical perspectives: VRD-Q (Statistical Rectification) : this variant performs in-place vector field alignment by employing asymmetric weight modulation based on value quantiles, which statistically filters sub-optimal regions without altering the underlying flow topology. VRD-R (Geometric Rectification) : this variant actively reshapes the flow’s topology, which constructs a value-gravity field that transports the generative trajectories toward a highly compact optimal support set, geometrically isolating them from sub-optimal modes. In summary, our primary contributions include: 1) Tracing OOD Mode Averaging: We theoretically trace the root cause of the OOD Mode Averaging problem in FQL-style distillation mechanism, revealing how its distillation objective interacts with latent fusion to generate invalid OOD actions on multi-modal data. 2) The VRD Framework: We propose Value-Rectified Distillation (VRD) with two implementations VRD-Q and VRD-R, reformulating offline policy distillation as a value-guided trajectory alignment problem to safely extract high-value policies without mode averaging. 3) Empirical Validation: Extensive evaluations demonstrate that VRD-Q and VRD-R effectively mitigate this OOD issue, outperforming or performing competitively with existing generative baselines across various continuous control and planning tasks.

VRD-R (Geometric Reshaping): Rescales high-value latent vectors into a compact region around the origin. It acts as a symmetry-breaker to isolate a single, highly stable peak mode, which enable VRD-R for continuous control tasks where single-mode precision and stability are prioritized (e.g., standard D4RL locomotion). sections.heading: Gaussian Policies.
sections.text: Traditional offline RL methods often rely on Gaussian distributions to parameterize the policy. This category includes standard Behavior Cloning ( BC [ 16 ] ) as well as prominent value-based algorithms like Implicit Q-Learning ( IQL [ 14 ] ) and ReBRAC [ 23 ] . While Gaussian policies are computationally efficient, in complex offline datasets where behavior is often multi-modal or skewed, Gaussian-based actors suffer from limited expressivity [ 21 ] , often leading to mode-averaging and suboptimal performance when the data distribution is non-Gaussian.

sections.heading: Diffusion Policies.
sections.text: To overcome the expressivity bottleneck, recent works such as IDQL [ 9 ] , SRPO [ 2 ] , and CAC [ 5 ] leverage the power of score-based diffusion modeling to capture highly complex and multi-modal action distributions. However, directly optimizing an iterative diffusion process to maximize a Q-function remains challenging, often requiring unstable backpropagation through the sampling steps or complex reward-guided sampling techniques [ 12 ] .

sections.heading: Flow Policies.
sections.text: Flow matching [ 18 ] has emerged as a compelling alternative to diffusion, which is simpler to train and faster to infer. To address the difficulty of directly optimizing iterative flow models, Flow Q-Learning ( FQL ) [ 21 ] proposed distilling an expressive one-step policy from a flow-matching model guided by RL objectives, along with two variants: FAWAC [ 1 ] and FBRAC [ 25 ] , which bridges the gap between expressivity and efficiency. More recently, Guided Flow Policy ( GFP ) [ 24 ] and Decision Flow ( DF ) [ 11 ] develops tailored optimization techniques, focusing on specifically extracting high-value actions within the flow framework.

sections.heading: 5.1 Visualizing latent rectification on toy examples (RQ1)
sections.text: To empirically evaluate how our methods manipulate the latent space to extract optimal policies, we construct a 2D bi-modal toy environment. The dataset comprises actions sampled from an optimal mode at [ − 2.0 , 0.0 ] [-2.0,0.0] and a sub-optimal mode at [ 2.0 , 0.0 ] [2.0,0.0] , with isotropic Gaussian noise, where the corresponding value landscape is simulated using a mock Q-function strictly centered at [ − 2.0 , 0.0 ] [-2.0,0.0] . Figure 3: Visualizing results on toy examples with 2D multi-modal data. Although the baseline flow model perfectly replicates the offline dataset by indiscriminately absorbing both modes (Figure 3 a), it suffers from latent fusion at the boundary between the optimal (red) and sub-optimal (blue) latent variables ( Z Z ), where the entanglement induces OOD action interpolations, hindering clear optimal mode distillation and exacerbating the risk of OOD mode averaging in FQL-style behavior distillation (Figure 3 b). In contrast, the proposed VRD successfully extract a strictly optimal policy (Figure 3 c, d). Specifically, VRD-Q performs statistical filtering by dynamically truncating distillation weights in low-value latent regions, which severs the gradient flow for sub-optimal actions, forcing the standard Gaussian prior to map exclusively to the optimal mode. Conversely, VRD-R geometrically reshapes the latent topology via value-guided spatial transportation. It attracts optimal latent variables toward the origin while expelling sub-optimal ones to the periphery. By sampling from a low-temperature Gaussian prior during zero-shot inference, VRD-R isolates optimal trajectories, verifying the efficacy of both rectification strategies.

sections.heading: 5.3 Deep dive into multi-modal datasets (RQ3)
sections.text: To evaluate robustness against multi-modal distributions, we construct mixed datasets combining expert (optimal) and random (sub-optimal) trajectories, as discussed in [ 13 , 27 ] . Maintaining a 1,000,000-sample buffer, we vary the ratio of random samples from 50 % 50\% to 90 % 90\% , progressively diminishing the expert mode’s presence, which serves as a rigorous stress test to determine if our mechanisms can successfully isolate the vanishing optimal mode from multi-modal data. Figure 4: Results over different scales of multi-modal datasets. From Figure 4 , we observe that both the statistical filtering of VRD-Q and the geometric reshaping of VRD-R exhibit a more gradual performance degradation as the proportion of sub-optimal modes (i.e., the random sample ratio) increases. Specifically, on the ’halfcheetah-mix’ and ’walker2d-mix’ datasets, both VRD variants significantly outperform the CQL and FQL baselines. This improved robustness is likely because agents in these two environments are more susceptible to overfitting to sub-optimal noisy data, a vulnerability that the proposed VRD methods appear to effectively mitigate.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: This paper proposes the Value-Rectified Distillation (VRD) framework, reformulating policy distillation as a value-guided trajectory alignment process to solve the latent fusion problem in offline RL over multi-modal dataset. VRD-Q and VRD-R mitigate OOD Mode Averaging problem via statistical filtering and geometric reshaping respectively. Experiments show VRD successfully decouples the high-value behavior mode from the multi-modal data, which enables VRD outperform baselines on various benchmarks and datasets, demonstrating exceptional robustness for sub-optimal data noise.

sections.heading: Limitations (see Appendix D ).
sections.text: The proposed VRD relies on the underlying value network’s accuracy, where severe Q-value overestimation may mislead the alignment process. Future work could explore more robust value estimation or extend this framework to discrete action spaces.

sections.text: The MuJoCo task suite within the Minari dataset [ 26 ] serves as a standardized benchmark widely adopted in offline reinforcement learning (RL) research. Developed by the Farama Foundation as a modern successor to the D4RL dataset, these tasks are built upon classic physics simulation environments, including HalfCheetah , Hopper , and Walker2d . Minari provides a tiered classification system to evaluate algorithms across varying data qualities: • Simple Datasets : These are primarily generated by random or early-stage training policies. They contain a high volume of low-value, exploratory trajectories characterized by a divergent distribution and a low signal-to-noise ratio, testing an algorithm’s ability to extract fundamental control logic from poor-quality data. • Medium Datasets : Collected from policies at intermediate performance levels, these datasets are goal-oriented but frequently contain sub-optimal actions and failed attempts. They serve as a core benchmark for evaluating whether an algorithm can effectively isolate optimal modes and outperform the data average. • Expert Datasets : Generated by fully converged, high-performance policies, these represent optimal behavior with a narrow, high-quality distribution. They are designed to verify if an algorithm can achieve high-precision policy alignment and maintain expert-level performance under limited data diversity. By adhering to the Gymnasium API and providing comprehensive metadata, Minari serves as an ideal testbed for evaluating capacity for mode separation and distributional correction within complex, multi-modal, and non-expert datasets. sections.heading: C.3 Full sensitivity analysis for hyperparameters
sections.text: To provide a comprehensive understanding of the stability and robustness of the Value-Rectified Distillation (VRD) framework, we conduct an extensive grid search on two primary hyperparameters: the quantile threshold τ \tau for VRD-Q and the truncation radius σ \sigma for VRD-R, alongside the balance coefficient λ \lambda . The results are visualized in Figure 5 and Figure 6 . Figure 5: Sensitivity analysis for VRD-Q.

sections.heading: C.3.1 Analysis of VRD-Q Sensitivity (Figure 5 )
sections.text: The experimental results on D4RL ‘medium‘ datasets (HalfCheetah, Hopper, and Walker2d) reveal several key insights for VRD-Q: • Inverted U-shape performance w.r.t. τ \tau : The performance generally follows an inverted U-shaped curve across all environments. When τ \tau is too small (e.g., 0.5 0.5 ), the statistical filtering is insufficient to suppress sub-optimal behavioral modes. Conversely, an excessively large τ \tau (e.g., 0.9 0.9 ) overly restricts the distillation weight, leading to a loss of distribution coverage and potential vanishing gradients. • Optimal τ \tau Region: The peak performance consistently resides in the range of τ ∈ [ 0.7 , 0.8 ] \tau\in[0.7,0.8] . This range effectively balances the exclusion of low-value "OOD noise" with the preservation of high-value multi-modal trajectories. • Robustness to λ \lambda : VRD-Q demonstrates relative stability across a wide range of λ \lambda (from 0.02 0.02 to 0.1 0.1 ). However, very large values of λ \lambda (e.g., 1.0 1.0 ) tend to degrade performance as the rectification term begins to dominate the Q-value maximization objective. Figure 6: Sensitivity analysis for VRD-R.

sections.heading: C.3.2 Analysis of VRD-R Sensitivity (Figure 6 )
sections.text: For the geometric rectification variant VRD-R, the sensitivity analysis highlights: • Criticality of Truncation Radius σ \sigma : Performance is highly sensitive to the scale of the latent prior during inference. When σ = 1 \sigma=1 (equivalent to standard Gaussian sampling), the performance is sub-optimal because the sampler hits the peripheral sub-optimal regions. • Optimal σ \sigma Scale: As σ \sigma decreases towards 10 − 4 10^{-4} , the performance significantly improves and stabilizes. This confirms that the value-guided gravity field successfully compresses high-value actions toward the latent origin, and a smaller σ \sigma ensures the sampler stays within this "expert core." • Environment Consistency: Similar to VRD-Q, the best configuration for VRD-R is relatively consistent across different locomotion tasks, with λ = 0.05 \lambda=0.05 and σ = 10 − 4 \sigma=10^{-4} providing the most robust results.

sections.heading: C.3.3 Practical Hyperparameter Tuning Suggestions
sections.text: Based on our empirical analysis, we offer the following guidelines for applying VRD to new offline RL tasks: 1. Tuning the Quantile Threshold τ \tau (VRD-Q): • Default: Start with τ = 0.7 \tau=0.7 . • High-Noise / Exploratory Datasets: While Theorem 2 suggests a larger τ \tau under an oracle critic, on noisy datasets (e.g., “random” or “medium-replay”) the learned Q-network inherently suffers from higher estimation variance. Setting τ \tau too close to 1.0 1.0 makes the suboptimal anchor weight 1 − τ 1-\tau vanishingly small, causing the actor to exploit spurious OOD Q-peaks and destabilizing training. Thus, we recommend decreasing τ \tau slightly (e.g., to 0.6 ∼ 0.7 0.6\sim 0.7 ) to retain a necessary behavioral regularization margin ( 1 − τ ∈ [ 0.3 , 0.4 ] 1-\tau\in[0.3,0.4] ) for training stability while still down-weighting suboptimal modes. • Expert / Structured Datasets: For datasets with high-quality demonstrations where value estimation is accurate and stable, a larger τ \tau (e.g., 0.8 ∼ 0.9 0.8\sim 0.9 ) can be safely employed to aggressively concentrate the policy onto the peak optimal trajectories without risking OOD divergence. 2. Tuning the Truncation Radius σ \sigma (VRD-R): • Default: Set σ = 10 − 4 \sigma=10^{-4} . • Geometric Adjustment: If the agent exhibits "mode collapse" (too little variety in actions), increase σ \sigma to 10 − 3 10^{-3} . If the agent still chooses sub-optimal actions in multi-modal settings, decrease σ \sigma to 10 − 5 10^{-5} to force more aggressive centering. 3. Tuning the Balance Coefficient λ \lambda : • We recommend λ ∈ [ 0.05 , 0.1 ] \lambda\in[0.05,0.1] . A smaller λ \lambda (e.g., 0.02 0.02 ) is preferred when the Q-function is well-trained and accurate. If the environment is complex and requires stronger regularization to prevent OOD mode-averaging, increase λ \lambda to 0.5 0.5 .

Task-specific tuning is strictly limited to the core hyperparameters of the VRD framework ( τ \tau for VRD-Q and σ \sigma for VRD-R) to adapt to the varying degrees of multi-modality, dataset quality, and environment complexity.

sections.heading: Appendix D Discussion
sections.text: While the proposed Value-Rectified Distillation (VRD) framework, including its two instantiations (VRD-Q and VRD-R), successfully addresses the fundamental Latent Fusion and Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Mode Averaging problems in flow-based offline RL, there are several limitations and open challenges that warrant further investigation.

sections.heading: 1. Reliance on Q-value Accuracy.
sections.text: The core mechanism of VRD inherently relies on the accuracy of the underlying value network to guide the trajectory alignment. Specifically, the quantile weight ω τ ​ ( z ) \omega_{\tau}(z) in VRD-Q and the geometric reshaping function Φ Q ​ ( s , z ) \Phi_{Q}(s,z) in VRD-R are directly derived from the estimated Q-values. If the Q-network suffers from severe OOD overestimation—a notoriously common issue in offline RL—the VRD framework might inadvertently align the generative flow toward falsely optimistic, low-density regions. Although our empirical results demonstrate robustness, future work could explore integrating more rigorous conservative value estimation methods (e.g., CQL-style penalties or uncertainty-aware ensembles) directly into the value-rectification functional to mitigate this risk.

sections.heading: 2. Restriction to Continuous Action Spaces.
sections.text: The theoretical foundation of VRD (as proven in Theorem 1 and 2 ) and the Flow Matching parameterization are built strictly upon continuous vector fields and continuous topological mappings. Consequently, the current framework is restricted to continuous control tasks. Extending this value-guided flow rectification paradigm to discrete action spaces (e.g., Atari games or discrete routing problems) is non-trivial. Future research could explore incorporating Categorical Flow Matching or Discrete Diffusion processes, adapting the latent distribution alignment functional to discrete categorical probabilities.

sections.heading: 3. Potential Diversity Collapse in VRD-R for Multi-Modal Experts.
sections.text: By design, the geometric rectification in VRD-R utilizes a centripetal gravitational field, as Eq.( 12 ), that maps all high-value behaviors towards the origin of the latent space ( ‖ z ‖ ≈ 0 \|z\|\approx 0 ). While this strictly isolates optimal modes from sub-optimal noise, it may lead to an unintended diversity collapse if the underlying optimal behavior itself is inherently multi-modal (i.e., there are multiple distinct but equally optimal strategies). By forcing all optimal trajectories into a single highly compact hypersphere, VRD-R might destroy the topological diversity of expert modes. VRD-Q avoids this by employing an in-place statistical filtering, which explains why VRD-Q generally exhibits broader stability across diverse environments. Future iterations of VRD-R could explore multi-centric gravitational fields (e.g., using Gaussian Mixture priors) to preserve expert multi-modality.

Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. • All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced. • All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. • The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition. • Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. • Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Detailed experimental settings are referenced in the main text. These are extensively expanded upon in Appendices C, providing the necessary hyperparameters, optimizers, and architectural configurations. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. • If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable. • Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. • While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. (c) If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset). (d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. Answer: [Yes] Justification: Our paper reports appropriate information about statistical significance of the experiments. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper. • The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). • The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.) • The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). • It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. • It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 arXiv:2610.29075v1 [cs.LG] 21 Oct 2026 Value-Rectified Distillation for Flow-based Offline Reinforcement Learning Ke Jiang Affiliation: College of Computer Science and Technology, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics Affiliation: MIIT Key Laboratory of Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence Affiliation: Graduate School of Information Science and Technology, The University of Osaka Email: kejiang@nuaa.edu.cn Wen Jiang Affiliation: College of Computer Science and Technology, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics Affiliation: MIIT Key Laboratory of Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence Email: darren.jum@nuaa.edu.cn Yoshinobu Kawahara Affiliation: Graduate School of Information Science and Technology, The University of Osaka Affiliation: Center for Advanced Intelligence Project, RIKEN Email: kawahara@ist.osaka-u.ac.jp Xiaoyang Tan Affiliation: College of Computer Science and Technology, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics Affiliation: MIIT Key Laboratory of Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence Email: x.tan@nuaa.edu.cn Abstract We aim to address the problem of Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Mode Averaging , a critical problem that emerges when distilling Flow Matching (FM) based behavior policies in offline Reinforcement Learning (RL): When learning over multi-modal datasets, standard distillation inadvertently forces the policy to interpolate across different behavioral modes, causing the generated actions to collapse into invalid, OOD regions. To resolve this, we propose Value-Rectified Distillation (VRD) , a novel framework that reformulates offline policy distillation as a value-guided generative trajectory alignment problem. By employing a dynamic coupling mechanism, VRD actively rectifies flow dynamics to explicitly decouple distinct behavioral modes, cleanly isolating high-value actions. Specifically, we instantiate VRD through two complementary algorithms: VRD-Q , which utilizes value-quantile behavior distillation to statistically filter out low-value behaviors, and VRD-R , which reorganizes the latent space to geometrically isolate high-value generative trajectories from the FM-based behavior policy. Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that VRD improves existing generative baselines across diverse continuous control and planning tasks on the D4RL, OGBench, and Minari benchmarks, especially over those multi-modal, non-expert datasets. 1 Introduction Offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) aims to derive a high-capacity policy from a fixed, pre-collected dataset without further environment interaction [ 17 , 15 ] , which is particularly vital for the applications where online exploration is costly or hazardous. Recently, generative models, particularly Flow Matching (FM) [ 18 ] , have emerged as a powerful alternative to traditional Diffusion-based methods [ 9 , 2 , 5 ] , where FM-based policies, such as Flow Q-Learning (FQL) [ 21 ] , offer significant advantages in modeling complex, multi-modal behavior distributions while circumventing the training instabilities typically associated with backpropagating through ODE solvers. Figure 1: Problem of Latent Fusion (left) and the OOD Mode Averaging problem caused by FQL-style behavior distillation (right). Despite their empirical promise, we identify a fundamental pathology in how current flow-based RL frameworks distill high-value actions from multi-modal behavior policies. Specifically, when learning from multi-modal data, our analysis reveals that Flow Matching networks inherently suffer from Latent Fusion : the topological entanglement between the generative trajectories of optimal and sub-optimal behavioral modes, caused by the vector field’s training dynamics, as is shown in Figure 1 (left). In previous works, like FQL [ 21 ] , it first pre-trains a behavior flow policy to capture the full multi-modal behavior distribution [ 4 ] from the dataset, and subsequently applies Q-value guidance to distill the optimal policy. However, because such distillation operates on a continuous vector field where trajectories are already topologically entangled by the MLE pre-training, the Q-guided objective, as is shown in Figure 1 (right), inadvertently forces the sampled actions to linearly interpolate across distinct modes during inference, which triggers the OOD Mode Averaging disaster, where it is risky for the generated actions to collapse into low-density regions of the state-action manifold, ultimately causing performance degradation. Although recent approaches like Guided Flow Policy (GFP) [ 24 ] incorporate reward information to amplify optimal behavior modes in FM-based behavior policy, their FQL-style distillation mechanism still suffers from OOD Mode Averaging . To address this issue, our core insight is that during the distillation phase, policy refinement must go beyond simply cloning from FM-based behavior policy; rather, it inherently requires rectifying the flow dynamics to explicitly decouple distinct behavioral modes along the data manifold. Therefore, we introduce Value-Rectified Distillation (VRD) , a novel framework that reformulates offline policy distillation as a value-guided trajectory alignment problem, of which the core lies in a dynamic coupling mechanism that precisely modulates the flow dynamics to explicitly decouple and exclude sub-optimal behavioral modes, ensuring that the generated actions are confined to the optimal action manifold during inference. To instantiate this unified framework, we derive two distinct algorithms from complementary mathematical perspectives: VRD-Q (Statistical Rectification) : this variant performs in-place vector field alignment by employing asymmetric weight modulation based on value quantiles, which statistically filters sub-optimal regions without altering the underlying flow topology. VRD-R (Geometric Rectification) : this variant actively reshapes the flow’s topology, which constructs a value-gravity field that transports the generative trajectories toward a highly compact optimal support set, geometrically isolating them from sub-optimal modes. In summary, our primary contributions include: 1) Tracing OOD Mode Averaging: We theoretically trace the root cause of the OOD Mode Averaging problem in FQL-style distillation mechanism, revealing how its distillation objective interacts with latent fusion to generate invalid OOD actions on multi-modal data. 2) The VRD Framework: We propose Value-Rectified Distillation (VRD) with two implementations VRD-Q and VRD-R, reformulating offline policy distillation as a value-guided trajectory alignment problem to safely extract high-value policies without mode averaging. 3) Empirical Validation: Extensive evaluations demonstrate that VRD-Q and VRD-R effectively mitigate this OOD issue, outperforming or performing competitively with existing generative baselines across various continuous control and planning tasks. 2 Preliminaries and motivation 2.1 Offline RL and Flow Q-Learning Suppose a Markov Decision Process ℳ = ( 𝒮 , 𝒜 , r , ρ , p ) \mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},r,ho,p) , then the goal of offline RL is to learn a policy π \pi that maximizes the expected cumulative discounted return using a static dataset 𝒟 \mathcal{D} collected by a behavioral policy. The observation that standard Euclidean distillation is vulnerable to mode averaging on multi-modal datasets motivates our Value-Rectified Distillation (VRD) framework. Traditional offline RL methods often rely on Gaussian distributions to parameterize the policy. This category includes standard Behavior Cloning ( BC [ 16 ] ) as well as prominent value-based algorithms like Implicit Q-Learning ( IQL [ 14 ] ) and ReBRAC [ 23 ] . While Gaussian policies are computationally efficient, in complex offline datasets where behavior is often multi-modal or skewed, Gaussian-based actors suffer from limited expressivity [ 21 ] , often leading to mode-averaging and suboptimal performance when the data distribution is non-Gaussian. Diffusion Policies. To overcome the expressivity bottleneck, recent works such as IDQL [ 9 ] , SRPO [ 2 ] , and CAC [ 5 ] leverage the power of score-based diffusion modeling to capture highly complex and multi-modal action distributions. However, directly optimizing an iterative diffusion process to maximize a Q-function remains challenging, often requiring unstable backpropagation through the sampling steps or complex reward-guided sampling techniques [ 12 ] . Flow Policies. Flow matching [ 18 ] has emerged as a compelling alternative to diffusion, which is simpler to train and faster to infer. To address the difficulty of directly optimizing iterative flow models, Flow Q-Learning ( FQL ) [ 21 ] proposed distilling an expressive one-step policy from a flow-matching model guided by RL objectives, along with two variants: FAWAC [ 1 ] and FBRAC [ 25 ] , which bridges the gap between expressivity and efficiency.
